lessons.title: Reading what code really does
lessons.body: The bare-metal track: compile your own small C programs, then read what they became. This is how you build the muscle that closed-source and exploitation work both need - and it never goes stale.

tools.name: gdb (with pwndbg/GEF)
tools.what: The GNU debugger: step through a program instruction by instruction, inspect registers and memory, set breakpoints. The pwndbg/GEF add-ons make it far friendlier for security work.
tools.legal: Only run this against machines you own or have explicit written permission to test. Scanning or attacking other systems is illegal.
tools.install: `sudo apt install gdb`; then install pwndbg or GEF.
try: # break main ; run ; info registers ; x/8x $sp
tools.exercise: Write a 10-line C program, compile with -g, and step through main in gdb. Watch the stack change as you call a function. That picture is the foundation of exploitation.

tools.name: Ghidra
tools.what: The NSA's free reverse-engineering suite. Disassembles and decompiles a binary into readable C-like pseudocode, so you can study what a program does without source.
tools.legal: Only run this against machines you own or have explicit written permission to test. Scanning or attacking other systems is illegal.
try: # open a small binary YOU compiled and compare Ghidra's decompilation to your source
tools.exercise: Compile a tiny program, open it in Ghidra, and match the decompiled output back to your own code. Doing this on code you wrote builds intuition fast.

tools.name: AFL++
tools.what: A coverage-guided fuzzer: it mutates inputs by the millions and watches which ones reach new code or crash the target. Your optimization background fits here - a fuzzer is a search algorithm over the input space.
tools.legal: Only run this against machines you own or have explicit written permission to test. Scanning or attacking other systems is illegal.
tools.install: `sudo apt install afl++` or build from source.
tools.exercise: Write a small C parser with a deliberate bug, fuzz it with AFL++, and catch the crash. Then fix it and confirm the crash is gone. That loop is real vulnerability research in miniature.
